title: Morrissey Cancels Las Vegas Residency Days Before Showtime Due to ‘Unforeseen Logistical Issues’
description: Morrissey has canceled his four-date Las Vegas residency at The Wynn just a week before showtime, Rolling Stone reports. The musician cited “unfores
body:
Morrissey has canceled his four-date Las Vegas residency at The Wynn just a week before showtime, Rolling Stone reports. The musician cited “unforeseen logistical issues” as the reason for the sudden cancellation.

	The former Smiths frontman was set to play four shows at The Wynn’s Encore Theater starting Aug. 14. Ticket buyers were informed via email on Friday that all nights have been wiped. No reason was given as to why Morrissey shut down the Vegas residency outside of the unnamed “logistical issues.”
	

	“Hello, we regret to inform you that Morrissey – Live in Concert, scheduled for August 14, 15, 18, and 19 at Encore Theater at Wynn Las Vegas, has been canceled,” the email read. “Due to unforeseen logistical issues, the scheduled Las Vegas residency cannot take place.”


	The residency has been scrubbed from The Wynn’s website, and a listing on Ticketmaster’s page reads, “Unfortunately, the Event Organizer has had to cancel your event.” Earlier Saturday morning, Morrissey’s website still had the shows listed, but they’ve since been taken down. Morrissey’s next dates include Sept. 19 at Chicago’s Riot Fest, Sept. 22 at Shea’s Buffalo Theatre in Buffalo, N.Y. and Sept. 26 at Brooklyn’s CBGB Festival.

	Rolling Stone reported that Morrissey has made a habit of canceling shows, canceling 22 performances and postponing 10 others in 2025 alone. Several of his other cancellations have also had slightly vague explanations, including “reasons completely beyond our control,” “sleep deprivation” and “adverse reaction to a prescription medication.”
	

	Morrissey last performed on Aug. 1 in Portugal.

title: L.A. Jazz Festival, Which Was Supposed to Feature John Legend, Janelle Monáe and Hundreds More, Canceled at the Last Minute
description: The inaugural LA Jazz Fest, set for Aug. 7 to 23 and promising major events including a two-day concert at Dockweiler Beach with stars like John Leg
body:
The inaugural LA Jazz Fest, set for Aug. 7 to 23 and promising major events including a two-day concert at Dockweiler Beach with stars like John Legend, Janelle Monáe, Parliament/Funkadelic and Raphael Saadiq — was canceled Thursday at the very last minute, and commenters online are already comparing it to the famously doomed Fyre Festival.

	Organizer Martin Ludlow, a former L.A. city council member (who later pleaded guilty in state and federal courts after being accused of using union workers and money for his campaign), had promoted the LA Jazz Fest as a major citywide event, including free jazz performances in parks across the region, late-night shows in local clubs and a “Caribbean Street Carnival” block party in Venice on Aug. 21.
	

	The ambitious festival also promised a youth jazz camp and youth jazz intensive/master class, and seminars on the state of jazz in America. The LA Jazz Fest was supposed to kick off on Aug. 7 with an opening night event in Leimert Park Village with acts including Lalah Hathaway, Kenyon Dixon, Chief Adjuah and Pete Escovedo.


	The main event, however, was supposed to be a “Jazz on the Beach” two-day event at Dockweiler Beach on Aug. 22 and 23. Other acts scheduled included Charlie Wilson, Ezra Collective, Free Nationals, Poncho Sanchez and Big Freedia. The event even boasted that it had organized parking at the Forum, with shuttles “along a closed-off route designed to skip the traffic entirely” to the concert.

	Ludlow announced the event at a City Hall press conference in February, which was attended by Mayor Karen Bass. The LA Jazz Fest said it expected to attract 250,000 attendees and had been promoting the event up until just days ago. 
	

	By Friday, the LA Jazz Fest website had been scrubbed, with only a cryptic message that said, “August 22-23. Updated event info coming soon.” On the LA Jazz Festival‘s instagram page, comments had been removed from posts that still remained and touted a wide variety of events that now appear to not be happening.

	Reps for the organizers did not respond to a request for comment by Variety, but in a statement, Ludlow told the Los Angeles Times, “Due to significant, unanticipated last-minute public safety and municipal costs associated with the final permitting of the On The Beach Festival, we have reached the decision to unfortunately postpone this year’s inaugural LA Jazz Festival. Although this decision was an extremely difficult one to reach, our commitment to the audiences and artists participating in the festival is to have a first-class experience worthy of the great legacy of jazz and our great city. We were encouraged by the enthusiastic support of the artists on the bill, the fans and our sponsors for this inaugural event, and we look forward to presenting all of the components of this incredible cultural opportunity for Los Angeles and the world in 2027 and beyond.”

	But the reaction was a mix of anger and frustration among artists who had already traveled to Los Angeles from abroad to take part in the event, as well as vendors who had already purchased stock to sell at the now-canceled festival.

	“Not cool for us musicians who lost money on flights and rehearsals for this,” wrote one musician on CBS LA’s Instagram page. Added another: “They canceled a big band I play with! Terribly disorganized … a real train wreck.” CBS LA News spoke to jazz musician Isiah Collier, “who landed in Los Angeles on Friday after a long tour in Europe. He was scheduled to perform this weekend at the inaugural LA Jazz Festival, but at the last minute, he found out his and dozens of other performers’ gigs were canceled.”

	On KTLA’s Instagram, a rep from SB Music Management wrote, “Are they going to pay back all of the jazz musicians/crew etc. from the costs incurred, because they canceled with no notice? Too late for musicians to get money back from hotels and flights! Not just from that final weekend but the 17 days of concerts leading up to it?”

title: Giovanni Tortorici on Working With Monica Bellucci Who Plays an ‘Eccentric’ Aristocratic Matron in His Luca Guadagnino-Produced Film ‘Ketticè’
description: Emerging Italian director Giovanni Tortorici, whose feature debut “Diciannove” made a splash last year after launcing from the Venice Horizons secti
body:
Emerging Italian director Giovanni Tortorici, whose feature debut “Diciannove” made a splash last year after launcing from the Venice Horizons section, is in competition at the Locarno Film Festival with his followup, “Ketticè,” a coming-of-age drama set in 2012 Palermo, featuring Monica Bellucci who is among the film’s few professional actors.

	“Ketticè” explores the dynamics between two local sixteen-year-olds, Ketty and Giulio, who are from very different social backgrounds. They build an exclusive friendship that largely consists of getting stoned on pot that they buy from a street dealer in a Palermo housing project, an act that gives them “a shared refuge in their search for freedom, away from the judging eye of the adult world,” says the synopsis.
	

	The film’s title, “Ketticè,” refers to Ketty’s nickname, in Sicilian dialect.


	Tortorici, who is 30, relied on street casting for most of the film’s roles, the main ones being Rachele Testagrossa and Salvatore Gallina, who respectively play Ketty and Giulio.

	He spoke toVariety about depicting young teens in Palermo circa 2012, a time “marked by political stagnation, cultural numbness and the first pervasive impact of social media,” working with Bellucci, and getting guidance from Luca Guadagnino.

	Your first feature “Diciannove,” which means “Nineteen,” is about a 19-year-old and somewhat autobiographical. This one is about two 16-year-old kids from different social classes in Palermo. Does “Ketticè” also stem from personal experiences?

	Yes, this film was born a bit by chance. After I made “Diciannove,” I came across a screenplay I’d written when I was younger, around 22, that was about 16-year-olds. I had zeroed in on lots of dynamics, expressions, mannerisms, that I’d actually even forgotten about. So I started thinking a lot about that period and everything that being 16 had entailed for me. Being in high school, growing up in Palermo, and so on. I wanted to delve deeper and reconstruct a bit of that whole reality. All those relationships and the powerplay that characterized that period. It gave me the opportunity to explore things that I hadn’t touched on in my previous film because, after all, it’s a much more ensemble-based work. And it’s less intellectual. Powerplay, as I was saying, at that age is much clearer. For example, in the protagonists’ relationship with parents, with school, with government control. When they smoke weed, they are always worried about being seen and being monitored by the police with surveillance cameras.
	

	Talk to me about Ketty. She likes to fight and is related to a member of the Mafia.

	Ketty comes from a very different background than Giulio in Palermo. She’s working-class Palermo, and her behaviour, attitude and approach to life are almost radically opposed to those of the upper middle class or the city’s aristocracy, which is where Giulio comes from. In short her psychology, her behaviour fit into a different mould than Giulio. For example, the fact that she likes to physically fight is in total contrast to Giulio’s upbringing. He’s see very physically controlled, with his mother telling him to keep his elbows down at the dinner table and not to gesticulate with his hands. In short, there is a clear contrast between these two characters which is why they are attracted to each other.

	Giulio’s mother is played by Monica Bellucci, one of the film’s few professional actors. Can you describe your inspiration for the character she plays and what is was like working with Monica?

	Let’s say that I drew a lot of inspiration from real life. I’ve known many of these upper-class Sicilian women. They have a very particular character. In public, they are very elegant and well-mannered attitude. But then in their private lives, within the walls of their homes, they become pretty eccentric and even slightly violent. I’ve known many of these women, and I think it’s a transnational, class thing, rather than a territorial thing just in Palermo. When we were thinking about who could play this role, it was a bit difficult to imagine a non professional actress, and that’s when I thought of Monica Bellucci. Having known her, both in person and on the screen, I could envision her very well as this character.

	How was it working with Monica?

	As soon as we started rehearsing she immediately confirmed to me that she had understood the character very well and very deeply, within her own psychology. I think she gave a very intelligent, very realistic interpretation, even if the character is a bit eccentric. I have to say that when I showed the film to people who also know this aristocratic world, they told me that they found a lot of truth in her performance.



	

									Courtesy PiperFilm
	



	Luca Guadagnino, who is your partner, has served as a producer on both of your features. Does he give you advice?
	

	I have to say that generally the type of advice Luca gives is very maieutic [relating to the Socratic method of helping a person bring forth hidden ideas and knowledge through questions]. In the sense that maybe he doesn’t tell you specific things about a certain problem, but he tries to draw them out from within you. Then, through dialogue, he helps you understand what you really want, or are looking for. What you think is right for the film. So he’s like a kind of psychoanalyst who can help you discern what might be an external influence, or what might be something you are holding back on out of prudence, or even cowardice. So I think that it’s quite special. It’s a method that values ​​the author’s personal point of view, and he has definitely given me a lot of help through this method.

	This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.



	

									Courtesy PiperFilm

schema.headline: Giovanni Tortorici on Working With Monica Bellucci Who Plays an ‘Eccentric’ Aristocratic Matron in His Luca Guadagnino-Produced Film ‘Ketticè’

title: Atlanta-Based Liaison Pictures Joins France’s Because the Night Productions on Locarno Match Me! Title ‘Behemoth Ann Holds a Seance’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: John Henry Hinkel’s Atlanta-based Liaison Pictures, behind Charlie Kaufman‘s “How to Shoot a Ghost,” has joined France’s Because the Night Productio
body:
John Henry Hinkel’s Atlanta-based Liaison Pictures, behind Charlie Kaufman‘s “How to Shoot a Ghost,” has joined France’s Because the Night Productions on the doc-feature “Behemoth Ann Holds a Seance,” currently taking part in Locarno’s Match Me! networking platform.

	Directed by Isidore Bethel, Vicki Bethel and Daniel Hymanson, “Behemoth Ann Holds a Seance” remembers Arthur Douglas Thayer, an artist, designer, writer and educator who spent a lifetime crocheting creatures. 
	

	After his death, his wife Vicki and son Isidore organize an exhibit of his artworks, complete with explorable digestive tracts, fantastical appendages, and detachable eyeballs. Their efforts bring this singular artist’s legacy to millions of passengers traveling annually through the world’s busiest airport in Atlanta.


	“After Doug’s death, filmmaking emerges as a remedy for Isidore, Vicki and Daniel,” explains Anne-Laure Berteau, founder of Because the Night Productions. “Shooting and editing become ways of rewriting their lives – of transforming sorrow into a story that transcends reality. Cinema here is a radiant force, connecting ghosts and the living, art and the everyday.”

	Liaison Pictures’ recent credits include Kaufman’s “How to Shoot a Ghost,” which bowed last year in Venice, and “Coroner to the Stars,” by Ben Hethcoat and Keita Ideno, about former Los Angeles chief medical examiner Thomas Noguchi, which premiered at the 2025 Slamdance Film Festival in L.A. Other works, such as “Shotplayer,” by Sam Shainberg, and Elena Parasco’s “I’m Not Home,” screened at SXSW and Tribeca, respectively.
	

	Founded in 2023 by Hinkel and  Andrew Ostapchenko, the boutique film production and finance company champions auteurs across all genres. Liaison Pictures serves not only as a bridge between capital and creatives, but as a comprehensive support system for artists to fully develop their stories and ideas, according to Hinkel. 

	The collaboration between Hinkel and the Bethels transcends normal industry partnerships.

	“Liaison’s John Henry Hinkel has known Vicki and Isidore Bethel for decades; he was classmates with Isidore in high school and at Harvard,” Berteau notes.

	“I relocated to my hometown of Atlanta to found my company,” Hinkel adds. “Not only does ‘Behemoth Ann Holds a Seance’ take place where I grew up, it also redefines the types of films that can be made here.”

	Atlanta Airport hosted the exhibition of Thayer’s work, a selection of his crochet snakes, dollies and other creatures, from December 2023 to April 2024.  

	Presenting “Behemoth Ann Holds a Seance” at Match Me! in Locarno, the producers are looking for potential production, distribution and world sales partners.

schema.headline: Atlanta-Based Liaison Pictures Joins France’s Because the Night Productions on Locarno Match Me! Title ‘Behemoth Ann Holds a Seance’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Cookie Queens’ Review: A Doc About Girl Scout Cookies, Produced by Meghan Markle and Prince Harry, Is Too Much of a Reality-Show Ramble
description: I’ve never seen a documentary about Girl Scout Cookies before, so I went into Alysa Nahmias’s “Cookie Queens” figuring that it might include, among
body:
I’ve never seen a documentary about Girl Scout Cookies before, so I went into Alysa Nahmias’s “Cookie Queens” figuring that it might include, among other things, a tantalizing history of this beloved American institution — a rundown of the nine current varieties of Girl Scout Cookie (my favorite: Samoas, obvi! With Tagalongs a close second), a survey of some of the dozens of discontinued flavors (Rasberry Rallies, we hardly knew ye), and — more to the point — a look at how Girl Scout Cookies came to be, how the Girl Scout Cookie season developed into a wholesome Middle American pastime, and what Girl Scout Cookies have meant, through the decades, to those of us who hungrily consume them and to all the girls who’ve devoted themselves to selling boxes of them.
	

	But no! “Cookie Queens” includes none of that stuff. The movie unfolds entirely in the present and never gives you even a fleeting sense of the past, of how Girl Scout Cookies rose in prominence to become the phenomenon they are today. (In case you’re wondering, they were launched in World War I to raise money for U.S. soldiers.) The opening credits, set to the Julie Ruin’s “Cookie Road,” which sounds like a great lost track from the B-52’s, play over black-and-white photographs and old film footage of Girl Scouts from bygone eras. But once the credits are over, the movie gets down to its single-minded theme and obsession: how Girl Scout Cookies, once a quaint piece of Americana, have lurched into their late-capitalist phase, with the girls who sell them vying to become champions by fashioning themselves into 12-year-old entrepreneurial go-getters.
	

	“Cookie Queens” opens with some major stats: how each year, the Girl Scouts sell over $800 million worth of Girl Scout Cookies, and they do it in six weeks. The film then introduces us to the four girls who are its principal subjects, and who will each set their sales goal and attempt to fulfill it through the duration of the Girl Scout Cookie season. There’s 12-year-old Olive from Charlotte, N.C., who still has a twinge of baby talk in her elocution but is already so media savvy that she sounds like an influencer; her goal is to sell 8,000 boxes of cookies. There’s 5-year-old Ara, who has diabetes (a fact the film focuses on with a touch of heavy-handed irony), but is a numbers-crunching dynamo who does Pilates. There’s 8-year-old Shannon Elizabeth from El Paso, Texas, whose goal is to sell 2,750 boxes (as Juliette Lewis said in “Natural Born Killers,” “You’re so specific”), though her mother warns her about the third-week dropoff, when the market for Girl Scout Cookies starts to get saturated.

	Then there’s Nikki, a rambunctious and highly competitive 9-year-old from Chino, Ca., with two older sisters, one of whom became Cookie Queen — a champion seller, with a (broken) green-and-gold trophy to show for it. The sisters now join Nikki at her sales table, one of them making up a jingle on the spot (“Come! Buy! Some Girl Scout Cookies! They’re only six dollars! They’re only six dollars!”). Nikki’s mother is there too, shouting, “We take cash and credit card.”

	“Cookie Queens” understands that all of this is a bit funny; that’s why it keeps punching up the action with an annoyingly cute musical score. Yet the film, which counts Meghan Markle and Prince Harry among its executive producers, is so focused on each girl’s odyssey of selling that there’s virtually no other dimension to it. As a director, Alysa Nahmias thinks like a reality-show producer — she frames the movie as a contest, inviting us to chortle in admiration at what eager-beaver achievers all four girls are. “Cookie Queens” never deviates from that one note. It’s like “Dance Moms” meets a preteen version of “The Apprentice” meets the 2002 spelling-bee documentary “Spellbound” (a much better film), all built around the hawking of tasty treats.

	The parents are more involved than they once were, or probably should be. But with this scale of salesmanship (thousands of boxes), they need to be involved. You’re required to buy the cookie boxes in advance, which prompts one mother to say that she might have to mortgage their house. The profit margin isn’t large: Out of the $6 that each box sells for, the Girl Scout gets to keep $1. The rest goes to the Girl Scout council. Olive, God bless her, says she thinks this is unfair (she’s right), and suggests that a 50-50 split would be more appropriate. For a moment, I thought that’s what the movie was going to turn into — a Girl Scout Cookie “Norma Rae.” But all of that gets dropped rather quickly. “Cookie Queens” is a movie about precocious American girls learning to work the system, not fight it.
	

	The closest the film comes to a moment of unguarded emotion is when a pal of Olive’s says, “I see you as not just a cookie seller. I see you as my best friend.” Awwww! But maybe she’s also giving Olive a word of warning. After appearing on a local TV show, Olive says she thinks the segment went well but that “it was just cookie trivia.” She says it wasn’t necessarily effective from a business point-of-view. You think: Who is this, Marc Andreessen? “Cookie Queens,” like its four young subjects, looks at boxes of Girl Scout Cookies and sees cold hard cash. But the tasty crunch of capitalism, in this case, is mostly in the eye of the beholder.

title: Olivia Wilde Says She’s Become ‘So Much More Romantic’ Because of ‘The Invite’: ‘It Melted the Cynic Out of Me’
description:
Olivia Wilde said she has become “so much more romantic” because of “The Invite.”

	“It’s melted the cynic out of me,” she said at Switzerand’s Loca
body:
Olivia Wilde said she has become “so much more romantic” because of “The Invite.”

	“It’s melted the cynic out of me,” she said at Switzerand’s Locarno Film Festival .

	“I have spoken to people who have been through so much with their partners, and people have been in marriages for 40, 50, 60 years. They told me it was a very honest depiction of their own experience of really having several relationships with the same person.”
	

	It’s Wilde’s third feature after “Booksmart” and “Don’t Worry Darling.”


	“The Invite,” where she also stars alongside Seth Rogen, Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton, takes place one evening when Joe and Angela (Rogen and Wilde) invite their upstairs neighbours Piña and Hawk for a dinner party.

	At first, she thought her hit film was about the end of a relationship. 

	“Now, I feel that it’s much more about whether a relationship can begin again with the same person, whether you can have multiple relationships with one person, and actually whether there’s more merit to that than I would have thought before,” she said. 

	The other unexpected thing?

	“I did not think we were making this movie for all ages. I thought that this would probably hit people in a very specific part of their lives that were somewhere similar to our parts of lives, and then I’ve been blown away by meeting all these young people. In the States, our biggest audience is under 35, and a huge chunk of them are in their twenties,” she admitted.

	“Their questions are not based in regret. They’re based in hope, and I have just been blown away by how advanced, how mature these audience members are in terms of the way they’re thinking about who they want to be individually, who they want to be in relationship to someone else. It’s made me less cynical across the board.”
	

	She added: “In terms of the reality of cinema today and the theatrical landscape, in terms of romance and whether or not it’s dead, in terms of young people and their appetite for adult kinds of storytelling, this whole experience has made me much more optimistic.”

	Wilde fought for the film’s theatrical release. 

	“It’s an ancient part of our culture as humans. We used to gather and tell stories, and laugh together – for thousands of years. But comedies have been relegated to this second tier that didn’t deserve theatres,” she noted. 

	“I have the benefit of hearing from audiences and hearing how cathartic they have found it to laugh at some of these things and to laugh with strangers, which is why we fought for theatrical.”

	“Today is very special for me, and for all of us, because I was hoping we’d be seen in a few theaters. Tonight, we’re going to watch it with 8,000 people and I actually can’t believe it.”

	Wilde admitted that seeing the film at Sundance convinced her it was the right choice. 

	“We felt the film had that chemical reaction with the audience. I thought: ‘This was magic, we have to listen to this and fight for it. If you don’t fight for it, they ‘bribe’ you to not take theatrical. But we were really lucky that our financier gave me the opportunity to make this decision, which is something I don’t take lightly.” 

	“We really believed that audiences deserve to discover this together. I’m obviously really passionate about it, but I was passionate about it with a lot of support, which was great because we were able to take the correct offer from A24 and they really do believe in the theatrical game. Filmnation Entertainment has made international deals around the world – all theatrical.”

	She also called directing “the most thrilling and most fun job anyone could have.” 

	“I love it more than anything. I’ve been waiting to do it my whole life and I took a long time to actually have the confidence to do it. I was 35 when I directed my first movie [‘Booksmart’], and I feel like my training in acting allowed me to speak the language of actors in a way that has been integral to the way I direct. I can empathize completely.” 
	

	“I always say that directing is like being multilingual – you have to be able to speak to each actor in the language of their specific training and experience. I think that the job of acting never actually ends, even if you’re not in the movie.”

	According to Wilde, each of the characters ended up being created by the actors. 

	“Penélope gave her so much specificity and Edward really transformed that character and gave him nuance. Seth is such a genius that he understood, at every point, how to make this mad, both maddening and totally lovable. He mixed all this vulnerability with sad rage. For me, it was a masterclass. There’s alchemy to it. I don’t know if it’s something you can create and as a director, you can only pray for an experience like that.”

	Initially, she wasn’t supposed to play Angela. 

	“It was the cast that asked me to play that role! I’m really happy they bullied me into it because I didn’t realize how much I needed to play her. It was very cathartic and fun, and I love her. I’ve never had this experience before where it felt like I knew her. She was so different than me in many ways, but I knew her completely,” she recalled.

	“This project was really singular because we had such a unique kind of chemistry. There was this like-minded dedication to the project that made the process of acting and directing, I think, a lot smoother. There was also the benefit of being able to be in the scenes and to, at times, make a fool of myself so that they knew it was okay for them to make a fool of themselves. You kind of jump first so everyone else is a little less nervous,” she laughed. 

	“I had an extraordinary cinematographer, Adam Newport-Berra, who had my back in a way that made it possible, as well as the rest of the crew. But I don’t know if I could ever do it again. I think I probably won’t! But I’m glad I did it this time.”

	Also because she discovered a new side to her acting

	“I think because I was directing myself, I didn’t tell myself not to be as expressive. I feel like I’ve been told to be less expressive since I was really young. It’s not necessarily ‘beautiful,’ in the very superficial sense of that word,” she said.

	“It sometimes involved directors telling me: ‘Your face can look quite intense.’ So many actors, so many women and probably just people in general, are told to be less. Part of getting older is getting rid of that.”
	

	She wanted the audience to see Angela’s “heart beating.” 

	“It was liberating to play someone that vulnerable. I think that people have always asked me to play tough people, and I don’t know why. I’m not very tough. I think that if most actresses direct, they do often show a side of themselves that they feel they haven’t been allowed to.”

title: Box Office: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Swings into Second Weekend With $43 Million on Friday
description:
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” showed no signs of slowing down as it entered its second weekend in cinemas.

	“Brand New Day” added $43 million at the
body:
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” showed no signs of slowing down as it entered its second weekend in cinemas.

	“Brand New Day” added $43 million at the North American box office on Friday from 4,487 theaters. By Sunday, the Marvel-Sony tentpole should swing to $143 million, which represents about a 60% decline from its record-breaking $360 million debut. Those earnings would push “Brand New Day’s” domestic haul to $653 million through weekend two.
	

	On Wednesday, “Brand New Day” overtook “Toy Story 5” as the highest-grossing movie of 2026. While it took “Toy Story 5” since June to collect its $1.067 billion, “Brand New Day” rocketed to $1.155 billion in just seven days. It crossed $1 billion in six days, becoming the second-fastest film to reach the milestone behind “Avengers: Endgame,” which made $1.2 billion in just three days.


	Second place went to “The Odyssey,” which grossed $8.8 million on its fourth Friday in domestic cinemas. By Sunday, Christopher Nolan’s Greek epic should pull in $30.5 million, dropping just 40% from last week’s total. Through the weekend, North American revenues for “The Odyssey” are expected to reach $460 million.

	Outside of the two powerhouse holdovers, there was a trio of newcomers that arrived at the box office on Friday: Searchlight’s “Super Troopers 3,” Universal’s “One Night Only” and Iconic Event’s “Ice Cream Man.”

	“One Night Only” did the best of the three, landing in third place with $2.8 million on Friday from 3,012 domestic screens. It’s expected to make $6 million by Sunday. Starring Callum Turner and Monica Barbaro, the rom-com follows two hopeless romantics who spark a connection on the one night of the year singles are legally allowed to have sex.
	

	“Super Troopers 3” pulled in $1.7 million from 2,760 North American theaters on Friday for a fourth-place finish. The Broken Lizard threequel, which once again follows the hijinks of a ragtag team of New England highway patrol officers, is projected to make about $3.9 million through Sunday. “Ice Cream Man,” an Eli Roth horror movie about an evil ice cream vendor, slotted in all the way in eighth place. The film earned $1 million domestically on Friday from 1,090 locations and should gross about $2.1 million through the weekend.

	Finally, “Toy Story 5” took fifth place, adding $1.15 million as it enters its eighth weekend in theaters. By Sunday, rivals have the legacy sequel earning $4.1 million, pushing its domestic haul to about $470.5 million

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Swings into Second Weekend With $43 Million on Friday

title: ‘Tony’ Star Dominic Sessa on How Being a ‘Liar’ Helped Him Portray Anthony Bourdain and Why the Film Foreshadows His Later Struggles
description:
For most actors, playing a real person in a biopic comes with an unrealistic amount of pressure.

	But because Matt Johnson decided to focus on just
body:
For most actors, playing a real person in a biopic comes with an unrealistic amount of pressure.

	But because Matt Johnson decided to focus on just one summer in 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain‘s life — long before the famed chef-turned-writer ever wrote “Kitchen Confidential” or became a household name — “Tony” star Dominic Sessa had a wide-open canvas.

	“I personally find it more interesting when you can reveal to the audience something that is not really known or hasn’t been focused on at all. Even for the biggest fans of Bourdain, they feel like they’re seeing something new here,” Sessa tells Variety. “It is fascinating and impressive, to an extent, to see actors and set designers recreate really iconic moments in history to an uncanny level. It’s something that people admire, I think it’s cool and can appreciate that. But I was grateful that we had the freedom to [instead] put a lot of our own stories into this.”
	

	Set in 1975, “Tony” is more coming-of-age hangout movie than traditional biopic. It follows Anthony Bourdain, who simply goes by Tony at the time, as he follows his older school crush, Nancy (Emilia Jones) to Provincetown, Mass., lying about winning a writing fellowship. He spends his summer there and, in a desperate effort to find a roof over his head, stumbles into the local kitchen of a seasoned seafood chef (Antonio Banderas). It’s a summer that changes Tony’s life forever as he meets the erratic Sal (Leo Woodwall) and other folks in the kitchen.


	Aside from the 2021 documentary “Roadrunner,” Bourdain’s life has been recounted largely through his own books like “Kitchen Confidential” and “Medium Raw,” making “Tony” the first fictional biopic about the Emmy-winning host. And the film gave Sessa, who had his breakout turn in Alexander Payne’s 2023 film “The Holdovers,” the opportunity to step into his first lead role.
	

	“I was skeptical of it at first when it was presented to me,” Sessa admits. “I thought in my mind it was going to be a whole biography of his life as he’s older, working as a chef and I’m like, ‘This is ridiculous. I can never do this.'”

	Meeting with Johnson, the Canadian filmmaker and writer behind “BlackBerry” and “Nirvana the Band the Show the Movie,” was what allowed Sessa to “get comfortable” about taking on the role.

	“I felt I actually had a way to understand the character that was relatable to me and true to the things that I’ve experienced,” he says of Johnson’s approach.

	Below, Sessa breaks down how being a “liar” helped him portray the famed writer and cook, working with mentor figures like Banderas and how the film foreshadows Bourdain’s later struggles in life with mental health and drugs.



	

					“Tony” director Matt Johnson, left, with Dominic Sessa on set.
									Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		What’s so notable about this movie is that it’s so laser focused on this one moment in Bourdain’s life. That’s not what we typically see from biopics these days.	

	I think it’s how biopics are most effective. We’re actually able to tell a story and we had a lot of freedom in that there’s not a ton of information about him at this time, footage or audio recordings of him or anything. There’s the specific details that you get from the people that remember him at the time, his own personal accounts, and that is all we had to work off of, really. And beyond that, we had so much freedom in crafting a sort of fictionalized version of what we could only imagine it might have been like from what he describes [in “Kitchen Confidential”] and the way he describes the people and the mentors around him. That just gave us so much creative space.
	
		As somebody who’s just a few years older than Bourdain during this time period, what specific experiences did you find the most relatable?	

	The character in the script, he’s not honest. He’s a liar and I think in my whole life, as a young guy, especially in high school and college, I would lie to people and over-inflate things and try to make myself seem more capable or intelligent than I actually am. I would go on dates with girls and use big words so that I would seem smart, you know? That sort of thing is something that a lot of young guys do. For me, the core of understanding and playing the character was thinking about the times in my life where I was kind of putting it on or being an imposter. Especially my high school environment, a lot of my friends came from very wealthy or famous families and grew up with a very specific lifestyle and I did not have that experience growing up. I felt embarrassed about that, you know? I felt I needed to present myself in a way or just not even talk about my family or home life at all just to protect my own ego. But that’s what you do when you’re young!
	
	
		How did reading “Kitchen Confidential,” which the film takes a direct quote from at the beginning, inform your portrayal?	

	For the audience and me, it justifies playing the character in a way that’s not necessarily super likable, at least not at first. At times I would feel like, “Oh, am I representing this person in a good way or in the best way?” I just reminded myself that I was doing it honestly. I was being the person that he described himself as.
	
		You guys shot in Provincetown. Did you come across any locals that knew Bourdain way back when?	

	There were tons of people; the owners of The Lobster Pot, a very famous restaurant; and the family that owns Spiritus Pizza, where we filmed at, all knew him and had a relationship with him at some point. We ate at this restaurant called Ciro & Sal’s very often, owned by the Luster Brothers who worked with Bourdain at that restaurant in the ’70s. I know Matt, when he was living in Provincetown for a bit, spent a lot of time talking to them specifically and getting their personal accounts of what happened — even remembering things differently than how Bourdain described it.
	
		What struck you about the stories they told you?	

	There was one instance where, in the movie, he grabs this hot iron pan and burns his hand. Larry Luster was explaining how that is not exactly how it happened. Bourdain had a tendency to make stories sound more interesting. Lies! It was a cool insight to learn.
	
		That adds another layer to the film, perhaps, and what it’s saying about this front Bourdain is constantly putting on.	

	Exactly! We really are just trying to tell a version of the story in the way that he would want to see it, in the way that he would like to remember it.
	
		What was the energy like filming the restaurant scenes? Were there any memorable dishes?	

	It was pretty chaotic, we very much felt like we were just working in a kitchen. They threw a bunch of real dirty dishes at me, and Matt was just like, “All right, clean! Antonio’s gonna throw some shit at you, yell at you, and Stavros is gonna make fun of you. Just take it in and receive it, but don’t say anything. Don’t open your mouth. Just be scared!” That’s how we filmed a lot of stuff. It felt very much in his style of filming where we had handheld camera ops with zoom lenses and we could just do whatever we wanted in the space.
	

	Matt and I instantaneously hit it off and had a very similar sense of humor. We really had a good understanding of each other’s personal lives; we talked about a lot of personal things when we first met. I just felt a lot of trust in him. I knew we were gonna be able to work together not only as partners on the movie, but as friends. We actually had a fun time working together. I can’t say that for everybody I’ve worked with.
	
		Did you learn to cook any dishes?	

	Antonio was a really good cook for sure, he owns eight restaurants in Málaga, Spain. He’s really talented at pretty much everything. Stavros got good at making lobster rolls, like 20 a day. And Leo was impressive with the oyster shucking. In the movie when he’s just flicking those things into the bucket, he’s legitimately doing it.
	
		Antonio’s Chef becomes a crucial mentor character to Bourdain. Did he also become a mentor figure to you as an actor?	

	I’m still so young. I don’t really feel like I have a method to what I’m doing and a locked-in process when I’m making a movie. Then someone like Antonio comes in and I’m listening to the questions he’s asking and I’m like, “Oh shit. I did not think about that at all!” When a real pro veteran comes in and they start working through the scenes with you, it makes it so much more exciting. I’m selfishly taking in all these insights that they’re able to have about the scene and use it. It makes me better. He’s also just a really nice guy. We had a young cast, for the most part, and he was the oldest one. He had more energy than all of us! He’s got a youthful way about him.
	
		It’s really striking the way that Chef and Nancy choose to show Bourdain kindness after the lies he tells them over and over. 	

	It’s interesting when someone who feels so separate from who you are and where you are in your life, like Antonio’s character, can have a deep impact on you. Ultimately, I think Tony’s decision to do this plan to steal this money was coming from a place of feeling, “These people are going to hate me anyway. There’s no saving me. It’s already over!” The fact that he experiences this moment of graciousness from two people he’s fucked over pretty bad is the reason he feels it’s necessary to do the right thing, for lack of a better term.
	
		And then we see Bourdain look around during that beach scene as it clicks for him how food brings people together. It’s a real community.	

	It’s realizing that I’ve had this experience in this place and this restaurant that is forever going to connect me to these people. They’re always going to be connected through that summer and that experience. For the rest of his life, he’s constantly searching for moments in time where he’s genuinely connecting with people through food.
	
	
		There were, of course, many struggles later in his life. In any of your research or prep, did you find it difficult to separate out those things for your performance?	

	Especially his battles with drug addiction and mental health problems, it wasn’t something that Matt and I really found we could relate to at all. I can’t say we thought too much about it when making it. But there are moments, of course, especially coming from Leo’s character where we see these hints of what we know is gonna come later in his life. That scene with Leo on the beach and even them all doing cocaine and shit in the kitchen, showing up to work hungover — all that stuff is flashes of things that we know are ultimately going to become a part of his life later.
	
		Did Matt write Leo’s character specifically to foreshadow that?	

	Yeah, Leo’s character was really intentional in that way, everything about him from being covered in tattoos. Matt and I were really specific about all this stuff. The first time that I smoke a cigarette in the movie is because Leo gives me one. That becomes something that’s so iconically Bourdain. Bourdain was open about his struggles with using heroin in his life, and Leo is the one that introduces him to the heroin dealer in Provincetown. He’s so much that chaotic side of him.
	
		This is such an exciting moment in your career. Since your breakout role in “The Holdovers,” how have you been navigating these past few years?	

	I don’t know. I’m really getting a better sense of what I’m good at, and what I haven’t explored yet that I know I’m capable of. I just did this crazy movie in Spain where I finally get to yell for the first time, like I never get to yell in movies and scream at people! I’m always kind of playing these really brooding, sad young guys. This movie was intentional in the way that it’s been a part of my life for so long. For the past two and a half years, I’ve been thinking about this movie and working with Matt on it. In the time since filming, I just tried to get on sets and be a part of movies with great actors, learning as much as I could. Knowing specifically that this movie was going to be a lot of pressure on me, I just wanted to be as prepared as possible.
	
		Who are some of your dream directors to work with next?	

	I would really like to work with Zach Cregger! When I was younger, I was a big fan of “Whitest Kids U’Know.” And then obviously “Barbarian” came out, and I was obsessed with that movie. And “Weapons” is probably one of my favorite movies in the last decade.
	

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘Tony’ Star Dominic Sessa on How Being a ‘Liar’ Helped Him Portray Anthony Bourdain and Why the Film Foreshadows His Later Struggles

title: Bill Maher’s Joke About Ariana Grande’s Weight Draws Groans From ‘Real Time’ Audience
description:
Bill Maher made a joke about Ariana Grande’s weight during Friday’s episode of “Real Time,” and drew mixed reactions from his live audience.

	“I ho
body:
Bill Maher made a joke about Ariana Grande’s weight during Friday’s episode of “Real Time,” and drew mixed reactions from his live audience.

	“I hope the aliens are here, I do. I hope they’re here and watching us and they’re going to save us,” Maher said during his opening monologue. “And, by the way, the administration this week, just a few days ago, maybe yesterday, unleashed a new trove of UFO files. Interesting things in there. Triangular craft, weird lights over an army base, a stick-like figure with large eyes. Oh, that was just an Ariana Grande video.”
	

	That joke landed, receiving laughs and applause from the crowd. However, the follow-up was met with gone-too-far groans: “Please, we kid. We kid. Maybe that joke will make her eat something.”


The White House released a new wave of UFO files. Sightings include a triangular craft in the sky, high-speed orbs near an army base, and a stick-like figure with large eyes, but that was just Ariana Grande. pic.twitter.com/buBBGk2Ze4— Bill Maher (@billmaher) August 8, 2026


	On Aug. 2, a rep for Grande announced that the multihyphenate is taking a “step back from visibility” after her Eternal Sunshine tour. The rep cited “ongoing public scrutiny as one of the reasons for the break.

	“Ariana will be taking a step back from visibility after she completes the Eternal Sunshine Tour,” Grande’s rep said. “She looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny. This tour has been a beautiful experience for her. She loves her fans and has loved every minute of this tour so much.”

	During a performance at Chicago’s United Center on Monday night, the “Wicked” star further explained her motivations for stepping out of the spotlight.
	

	“Sometimes when a story comes out that’s not directly from me, things can get a little blown out of proportion. So I just wanted to speak to my fans directly tonight because I love you so much. The announcement that was made yesterday was not a reactive or impulsive thing,” Grande told the crowd. “It is something that I had decided to plan that I had quietly made a long time ago and it’s a decision that was made from a thoughtful and empowered place.”

title: Anthony Michael Hall Says John Hughes Wanted a ‘Breakfast Club’ Sequel Where the Original Cast Is ‘In Their 30s’
description: “The Breakfast Club” star Anthony Michael Hall said during a recent appearance on “The Rich Eisen Show” that director John Hughes wanted a sequel in
body:
“The Breakfast Club” star Anthony Michael Hall said during a recent appearance on “The Rich Eisen Show” that director John Hughes wanted a sequel in which the group of troubled teens reunites as adults.

	“It was something that was on his mind, the idea of bringing back the ‘Breakfast Club,’” Hall said. “Like, those five characters reunited somehow later in their life and they’re in the workforce and they’re in their 30s.”
	

	Hall explained that his last conversation with Hughes, who died in 2009 from a heart attack, was in 1988, three years after “The Breakfast Club” hit theaters.


	“He called me with John Candy on the phone, and it was about 1988, and we just hung out on the phone for a couple hours, and he talked about [the sequel] at that time,” Hall added, “So I think that it was something he was playing with. I don’t know if he had written it or not.”

	Hall starred as the book-smart Brian Johnson alongside Judd Nelson, Molly Ringwald, Emilio Estevez and Ally Sheedy. The mid-’80s classic followed a group of teens from different very backgrounds who became unlikely friends after a day in detention.

	Hall also appeared in 1984’s “Sixteen Candles” and 1985’s “Weird Science” for Hughes. Hall recalled that the director approached him about the latter just a few weeks into filming “The Breakfast Club.”

	Hall remembered, “He goes, ‘I just came up with another idea for our next film.’ He goes, ‘It’s going to be you and this other kid. You’re going to create a girl in the computer.’ I’m like, ‘What?’”

schema.headline: Anthony Michael Hall Says John Hughes Wanted a ‘Breakfast Club’ Sequel Where the Original Cast Is ‘In Their 30s’

title: Morrissey Cancels Entire Las Vegas Residency One Week Before First Show
description:
Morrissey
                          Sin City Residency Scrapped at the Last Minute
body:
Morrissey
                          Sin City Residency Scrapped at the Last Minute
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 8, 2026
                            11:08 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Morrissey's latest Vegas gamble is a bust ... the singer has pulled the plug on his entire four-show Sin City residency just days before he was supposed to hit the stage.
      
    
            Ticket holders were informed Friday that Morrissey's run at the Encore Theater at Wynn Las Vegas was canceled due to "unforeseen logistical challenges," according to a Rolling Stone report.
      
    
            The former Smiths frontman had been scheduled to perform August 14, 15, 18 and 19.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The shows have disappeared from Wynn's entertainment calendar, while Ticketmaster now lists the events as canceled. So far, Morrissey's official website hasn't offered any more explanation for what exactly went wrong.
      
    
            Of course, Morrissey has had his share of canceled gigs ... including a March show in Valencia, Spain, which he said was rendered impossible after noisy festivalgoers outside his hotel kept him from sleeping.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            At the time, Morrissey's website said the sleepless night left him in a "catatonic state" ... and Morrissey called his hotel experience "indescribable hell," claiming it would take him a year to recover.
      
    
            As for Vegas ... looks like the house won before Morrissey even got to the table.

title: Florida Man Jailed For Allegedly Killing Cats With Blow Dryer and Rag Soaked in Bleach

Florida Man
                          Allegedly Killed Kittens With Blow Dryer, Rag Soaked In Ble
body:
Florida Man
                          Allegedly Killed Kittens With Blow Dryer, Rag Soaked In Bleach
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 8, 2026
                            5:21 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            David Charette is a Florida man who shouldn't be around cats ... because he allegedly killed some in a cruel way, using a blow dryer and a rag soaked in bleach. 
      
    
            Those are the ugly allegations Charette is now facing -- and more -- from the Lee County Sheriff's Office. On Thursday, Charette was arrested and booked in the Lee County jail for aggravated animal cruelty on $100,000 bail.
      
    
            Police body cam video shows officers checking on one of the kittens, then Charette being placed in the back of a squad car.
      
    
            According to police, deputies arrived at Charette's Fort Myers home after getting a tip that someone was hitting and drowning a 2-month-old kitten named Luna.
      

            Luckily, Luna was still alive and was taken to an animal hospital for treatment, cops said, adding that other felines in Charette's world weren't so lucky.  
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Cops say witnesses told them Charette abused and killed his cats to punish his daughter when she acted up. 
      
    
            During their investigation, police say Charette had allegedly killed 2 of his cats in the past year. In June, Charette allegedly suffocated a 1-month-old kitten with a bleach-soaked rag. In another incident, he allegedly burned up a 3-month-old kitten with a blow dryer.
      
    
            The sheriff's office says Charette buried both cats in his backyard, but the remains of only one were found as deputies searched his property.

title: 5-Year-Old Boy With Autism Found Dead in Pond Near Florida Home
description:
5-Year-Old Boy With Autism
                          Found Dead in Pond Near His Florida Home
body:
5-Year-Old Boy With Autism
                          Found Dead in Pond Near His Florida Home
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 8, 2026
                            1:03 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A frantic search for a 5-year-old boy with autism ended in heartbreak ... after authorities say he was found dead in a pond just 30 feet from his Florida home.
      
    
            The nonverbal child was last seen by his father around 5 AM Friday inside their Tampa-area home, according to Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister. His dad told investigators the two fell back asleep ... and when he woke around 9 AM, his son was gone.
      
    
            The father searched the home and discovered a screened-in area had been broken and pushed open. After looking around outside, he called 911.
      
    
            Over 140 sheriff's office units joined the search, along with aviation, drones, K-9s and a dive team. Chronister said a police dog repeatedly circled a retention pond about 30 feet behind the home ... leading divers to enter the water.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Shortly after 11 AM, a diver found the boy dead in about 5 feet of water, authorities said.
      
    
            Chronister said this was the second time in less than two months an autistic child drowned near the apartment complex ... and urged parents of children with special needs to get them swimming lessons, noting children with autism can be particularly drawn to water.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The sheriff said his entire department was grieving with the boy's family ... adding his "heart breaks that the outcome wasn't what we all prayed for."
      
    
            The investigation remains ongoing.
      
    
            The boy was only 5 years old.

title: 'Menace II Society' Star Samuel Monroe Jr. May End Up In Vegetative State, Tough Choice Looms
description:
'Menace II Society' Sam Monroe Jr.
                          May End Up in Vegetative State ...
body:
'Menace II Society' Sam Monroe Jr.
                          May End Up in Vegetative State ...
                          Medical Decision Looms
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 8, 2026
                            12:00 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 8, 2026
                                5:21 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Samuel Monroe Jr. remains hospitalized in Los Angeles on life support, in a medically induced coma ... and it's getting more apparent there may be no light at the end of the tunnel, his family tells TMZ.
      
    
            The actor best known for his work in "Menace II Society" has been hospitalized since April ... initially going in for a severe case of meningitis, which turned into MRSA pneumonia -- and from there, one severe medical issue after another piled up.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Samuel's wife, Shawna Stewart, tells TMZ ... Sam's brain continues to swell because ventricles have enlarged ... and they're not holding the cerebral fluid, which is resulting in seizures. He's undergone three brain surgeries, we're told.
      
    
            She also says his left lung has partially collapsed.
      

            We're told Sam continues to have CT scans to monitor brain activity ... but doctors feel he may end up in a vegetative state ... and the family is struggling with making a very tough choice.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As we reported ... the actor has been battling for his life for months in the hospital ... requiring multiple blood transfusions in a matter of days, as his body is decimated by MRSA pneumonia and meningitis, among other ailments. He's been placed on dialysis.
      
    
            Shawna tells us ... the family -- who launched a GoFundMe back in April -- is in agreement that Sam will undergo 3-4 more CT scans ... and depending on the results, they may have to make a heartbreaking decision.
